title: LangChain: LCEL, prompts, parsers, tools
seriesDescription: LCEL, tools, retrievers, tracing, StateGraph, reducers, checkpointers, human-in-the-loop and streaming. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Runnables and the pipe operator, prompt templates, output parsers, structured output and the tool-calling loop in LangChain for Python.
source: LangChain Python docs (docs.langchain.com, python.langchain.com), langchain-core 1.8 run locally; LangChain v1 migration guide

questions.prompt: A user asks for the weather in Paris and Rome in Fahrenheit. Turn 1: the model requests get_weather for both cities in one response. Turn 2: it requests convert_to_f for both in one response. Turn 3: it writes the final answer. How many LLM calls does the loop make in total?
questions.explanation: Each model response is one LLM call: two tool-requesting turns plus the final answer = 3. The 4 tool executions are ordinary function calls and are not LLM calls. Parallel tool calls in a single turn are what keep this at 3 rather than 5.

questions.prompt: chain = RunnableParallel(a=prompt1 | model, b=prompt2 | model, c=prompt3 | model) | merge_fn. You call chain.batch(inputs) with 4 inputs. Assuming merge_fn does not call a model, how many model calls are made?
questions.explanation: Each input fans out to 3 branches that each call the model once: 4 x 3 = 12. batch runs inputs concurrently but does not reduce the number of calls. This is the cost arithmetic to do before adding fan-out.

questions.prompt: model.with_retry(stop_after_attempt=3) wraps a model call that always raises a retryable error. How many times is the underlying call attempted before the error propagates?
questions.explanation: stop_after_attempt counts total attempts, not extra retries: 1 initial try plus 2 retries = 3. I confirmed it by running a failing RunnableLambda wrapped with with_retry.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: Calling model.bind_tools([add]) and invoking it does not run the add function.
questions.reason: The returned AIMessage carries tool_calls (name, args, id) that your code or a ToolNode must execute and send back as a ToolMessage.

whys.a: Right: the model only proposes calls; execution and the follow-up message are your job.
whys.b: R is the reason A holds, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: bind_tools only attaches the schemas to the request. The execute step is your loop or LangGraph's ToolNode, which also lets you validate and authorise each call.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: chain.batch(inputs) processes the inputs concurrently by default instead of one after another.
questions.reason: RunnableParallel runs its branches concurrently on the same input.

whys.a: R describes a different feature (fan-out of one input), so it does not explain batch.
whys.b: Both are true but unrelated mechanisms: batch parallelises across inputs, RunnableParallel across branches.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Control concurrency with config={'max_concurrency': n} to respect provider rate limits. Both batch and RunnableParallel can multiply load on the provider.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: A function decorated with @tool exposes its name, type hints and docstring as the tool schema the model sees.
questions.reason: The docstring is optional, so a @tool function without one works without any extra arguments.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: A is true; R is false: I ran it and @tool raises 'Function must have a docstring if description not provided'.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: The docstring becomes the tool description the model uses to choose between tools, so write it like documentation for a colleague. @tool(description=...) is the alternative. In current langchain-core a @tool function with neither a docstring nor a description raises ValueError at definition time (checked by running it), which is why R is false.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: chain.invoke(x) returns an iterator that yields output chunks as they arrive.

whys.a: A is false, so a is wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so b is wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is false: invoke returns the final complete output; stream is the incremental one.

questions.explanation: Runnable methods: invoke (one input, final output), stream (chunks), batch (many inputs), and a-prefixed async versions: ainvoke, astream, abatch.

questions.prompt: Match each LangChain building block with its role.

right.text: Formats variables into a list of chat messages
Turns a model message into a plain string
Sends the same input to several branches and returns a dict
Wraps an ordinary function so it can join a pipe
Forwards its input unchanged, e.g. next to retrieved context

questions.explanation: Conversation storage is the job of a checkpointer or message history, not of these primitives.

questions.text: In LCEL the {1} operator composes runnables into a {2}, and calling .{3}() on it yields output chunks incrementally.
questions.explanation: prompt | model | parser builds a RunnableSequence. A dict or plain function next to a runnable is coerced, but two bare functions cannot be piped (TypeError).

questions.text: The model's AIMessage has a {1} list with the requested calls; after executing a tool you append a {2} that repeats the call's id in {3}.
questions.explanation: The id links each result to its request, which matters when the model asked for several calls in parallel.

questions.prompt: Given a chat model variable model, build an LCEL chain that formats the template 'Summarise: {text}', calls the model and returns a plain string, then invoke it with the text in the variable doc.

checks.label: builds a ChatPromptTemplate from the template
invokes with a dict containing text

questions.model:
prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template("Summarise: {text}")
chain = prompt | model | StrOutputParser()
result = chain.invoke({"text": doc})
questions.explanation: from_messages with a human tuple is equally valid. The input to a prompt is a dict whose keys match the template variables.
questions.starter:
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

questions.prompt: Define a LangChain tool get_order_status(order_id: str) -> str with a one-line docstring that returns 'shipped', then attach it to the chat model variable model so the model can request it.

checks.label: defines get_order_status with a str parameter

questions.explanation: Type hints and the docstring become the schema. A Pydantic args_schema is the alternative for complex arguments.

questions.prompt: Variables: ai is the AIMessage from the model, messages is the running message list and tools_by_name maps names to tools. Append ai, then for every requested call run the matching tool with the call's args and append a ToolMessage that echoes the call id.

checks.label: invokes the tool via tools_by_name and args

questions.model:
messages.append(ai)
for call in ai.tool_calls:
    result = tools_by_name[call["name"]].invoke(call["args"])
    messages.append(ToolMessage(content=str(result), tool_call_id=call["id"]))
questions.explanation: Then call the model again with messages. Passing the whole call dict to tool.invoke also works and returns a ToolMessage directly. In LangGraph the ToolNode does this loop for you.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of model.with_structured_output(Schema) over asking for JSON in the prompt and parsing it with a PydanticOutputParser?

options.text: It uses the provider's native tool-calling or JSON-schema mode, so output follows the schema more reliably.
options.why: Right: the constraint is applied by the API rather than hoped for in text.

options.text: It removes the need to validate the result, because the model can no longer produce wrong values in any field.
options.why: Validation is still needed: a schema-valid answer can still be factually wrong.

options.text: It always makes the call cheaper because the model is not sent any schema or instruction text at all.
options.why: The schema is sent to the model, as a tool or format definition, so tokens are still spent.

options.text: It removes the need to define any schema, because the model infers the fields from the prompt text alone.
options.why: A schema (a Pydantic class, TypedDict or JSON Schema) is still required: it is what is sent to the provider and used to parse the reply.

questions.explanation: Use native structured output when the model supports it and a parser with retry or fix-up logic as a fallback. Both still need validation.

questions.prompt: Which statements about LCEL runnables are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: batch returns the outputs in the same order as the inputs.
options.why: True: results line up with the input list.

options.text: A RunnableParallel returns a dict keyed by the branch names.
Piping two plain Python lambdas together with | works out of the box.
options.why: False: it raises TypeError; wrap one in RunnableLambda.

options.text: Streaming a component that cannot stream yields its whole output as a single chunk.
options.why: True: the fallback is one chunk at the end.

options.text: invoke returns an iterator of chunks, like stream.
options.why: False: invoke returns the final output.

questions.explanation: I checked the lambda and single-chunk behaviours by running them. Know the method family: invoke, stream, batch and async twins.

questions.prompt: In LangChain 1.x, which constructor is the documented replacement for the older langgraph.prebuilt.create_react_agent when you want a tool-calling agent?

options.why: Right: the v1 migration guide moves the prebuilt agent here and renames prompt to system_prompt.

options.text: langchain_core.agents.create_tool_chain, which builds a fixed sequence of calls and tools.
options.why: No such constructor: a fixed chain cannot loop between model and tools.

options.text: langchain.chains.AgentExecutor, which is the only supported agent runtime in 1.x.
options.why: AgentExecutor is the legacy runtime and is not the 1.x recommendation.

options.text: langgraph.graph.create_agent_node, which returns one node for a StateGraph.
options.why: Invented name: the prebuilt agent is a whole compiled graph, not a single node.

questions.explanation: create_agent is a compiled LangGraph graph, so checkpointers, streaming and interrupts still work. Older tutorials use create_react_agent; know both names because both appear in interviews and codebases.

questions.prompt: True or false: with_structured_output(Schema, include_raw=True) returns a dict with the keys raw, parsed and parsing_error, so a parse failure is reported in the dict instead of being raised.

options.why: Right: raw holds the AIMessage, parsed is None when parsing failed, and parsing_error holds the exception.
That is the documented shape of the include_raw=True output, so the statement is true.

questions.explanation: Handy when you want to log the raw message, retry on parsing_error, or read usage metadata from the raw AIMessage. Without include_raw the call returns only the parsed object.
